pos: n. (the ground; earth considered as the bed of plants)
etymology: French sol, Latin solum, the ground or bottom. In Ezekiel 17:8 it renders the Hebrew sadeh, a field.
biblical_def: Ezekiel's riddle of the two eagles and the vine turns on where the vine was planted: “It was planted in a good soil by great waters, that it might bring forth branches, and that it might bear fruit, that it might be a goodly vine” (Ezekiel 17:8). The vine is Zedekiah, set in Jerusalem under Babylon's oath, given every advantage a planting can have — good field, great waters, room to grow. And then he turned to Egypt for help, and the prophet asks the question the chapter exists to ask: “Yea, behold, being planted, shall it prosper? shall it not utterly wither, when the east wind toucheth it?” (Ezekiel 17:10). Good soil does not save a vine that breaks covenant. The Authorized Version uses soil once. The chapter does not end in withering, however; it ends with the LORD Himself planting: “I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it” (Ezekiel 17:22), a tender twig planted on a high mountain that becomes a great tree. The dictionary reads that last planting as messianic, as the New Testament and the Reformed tradition read it. Man's planting withered in good soil; God's planting grows.

corruption_paragraphs: The common error is to read Ezekiel 17 as pure political commentary — Judah caught between great powers, with no theological verdict. Ezekiel gives a verdict in plain words: Zedekiah despised the oath and brake the covenant, and the LORD says, shall he prosper? The chapter is about covenant-breaking, not statecraft.

What survives is the twig the LORD crops off and plants Himself, and the dictionary reads that planting as Christ and His kingdom.

etymology: Saxon westerne, from west. In Numbers 34:6 it describes the sea-border of Canaan.
biblical_def: The LORD gives Moses the survey of the promised land, boundary by boundary, and the west is the simplest line of the four: “And as for the western border, ye shall even have the great sea for a border: this shall be your west border” (Numbers 34:6). The Mediterranean is the wall. The Authorized Version uses western once, and it is in a title deed. God does not give His people a vague promise of land; He gives surveyed boundaries — south from the wilderness of Zin, west the great sea, north toward Hamath, east down the Jordan to the salt sea. The whole chapter opens, “this is the land that shall fall unto you for an inheritance” (Numbers 34:2), and the word fall is the language of the lot. The dictionary notes two things. First, the particularity: a covenant God deals in named rivers and fixed coasts, which is why the biblical narrative is history and not myth. Second, the direction of the promise. Israel's western boundary was a sea she never sailed; the gospel would go out across it to the nations, and the land that was once a border became a highway.

pos: v. (third person singular of whirl; turns rapidly round)
etymology: Saxon hwyrfan, to turn. In Ecclesiastes 1:6 it renders the Hebrew sabab, to go round or circle.
biblical_def: The Preacher's opening argument is drawn from nature, and the wind is his second witness: “The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north; it whirleth about continually, and the wind returneth again according to his circuits” (Ecclesiastes 1:6). The sun rises and sets and rises; the wind circles and returns; the rivers run to the sea and the sea is never full (Ecclesiastes 1:7). Three pictures of ceaseless motion that arrives nowhere. The Authorized Version uses whirleth once. The conclusion follows: “The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun” (Ecclesiastes 1:9). The dictionary reads Ecclesiastes as Scripture, not as a pagan fragment smuggled into the canon. Solomon is not denying God's providence; he is describing life under the sun — that is, life considered without reference to what is above it — and showing that it cannot be made to add up. The book ends where the argument has to end: fear God, and keep his commandments. The wind's circuits are not meaningless; they are meaningless to a man who will not look up.

corruption_summary: Ecclesiastes is widely read as canonical scepticism; it is inspired Scripture describing life under the sun, and it ends at the fear of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors are standard. The critical reading treats Ecclesiastes as a late, non-Solomonic, essentially sceptical work preserved for its literary interest; the dictionary holds Solomonic authorship and full inspiration. The devotional error quotes the vanity verses as though despair were the book's doctrine, and skips the conclusion of the whole matter.

The principle to recover is the phrase under the sun. The Preacher is conducting an honest experiment: granted a world and no God above it, what adds up? Nothing does. The wind whirls and returns; there is no new thing. That verdict is true, and it is the reason the last chapter says to fear God and keep His commandments.

pos: adj. (more remote; the further of two sides)
etymology: From far, Saxon feor, with a comparative ending. In Mark 10:1 it renders the Greek peran, beyond, across.
biblical_def: Mark marks a geographical turn that is also a turn in the ministry: “And he arose from thence, and cometh into the coasts of Judaea by the farther side of Jordan: and the people resort unto him again; and, as he was wont, he taught them again” (Mark 10:1). The Lord leaves Galilee for the last time and comes down the east bank — the farther side — toward Jerusalem and the cross. The Authorized Version uses farther as an adjective here alone. Two clauses in the verse deserve weight. The people resort unto him again: the crowds followed across a river to a new province. As he was wont, he taught them again: His settled habit was teaching, and He kept it with the cross a few weeks away. What He taught them first in this new place was marriage, and the Pharisees came tempting Him about divorce; His answer is the dictionary's standard on the question: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Mark 10:9). The farther side of Jordan is where the Lord Jesus laid down the creation ordinance of marriage against the permissions men had built on Moses.

corruption_summary: Mark 10 is the chapter modern teaching most often reinterprets to widen the grounds of divorce; the Lord narrowed them to the creation order.
corruption_paragraphs: The Pharisees asked whether it was lawful for a man to put away his wife, expecting a debate about grounds. Christ refused the frame and went behind Moses to Genesis: from the beginning of the creation God made them male and female. Every scheme that makes marriage dissoluble at will, or redefines the two whom God joins, is answered in that sentence — not by a stricter rule but by an older fact.

The principle to recover is that the Lord taught the creation ordinance as binding and as His own. Mark 10:6 and Mark 10:9 are the dictionary's standard: one man and one woman, joined by God, not to be put asunder by man.

pos: n. pl. (places of temporary dwelling; here, the remotest quarters of a territory)
etymology: French loger, to lodge, from loge, a hut. In 2 Kings 19:23 it renders a Hebrew word for the extremity or far lodging-place of a border.
biblical_def: Isaiah reports the LORD's answer to Sennacherib, and the answer begins by quoting the Assyrian's own boasting back at him: “By thy messengers thou hast reproached the Lord, and hast said, With the multitude of my chariots I am come up to the height of the mountains, to the sides of Lebanon, and will cut down the tall cedar trees thereof, and the choice fir trees thereof: and I will enter into the lodgings of his borders, and into the forest of his Carmel” (2 Kings 19:23). The lodgings of his borders are the furthest habitations of the land — the last outposts, the far corners. Sennacherib boasts that he will reach them all. The Authorized Version uses lodgings once. The reply is one of the most withering in Scripture: “therefore I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest” (2 Kings 19:28). The great king who meant to lodge at the ends of Judah went home the way he came, led like a beast. The dictionary notes the doctrine: the boasts of empires are quoted accurately in Scripture and then answered, and the answer is never a counter-boast from Judah but a word from the LORD of hosts.

pos: n. pl. (couplings; the places where parts are joined)
etymology: French joindre, Latin jungere, to join. In 1 Chronicles 22:3 it renders a Hebrew word for couplings or clamps.
biblical_def: David cannot build the temple, so he stockpiles for the son who will: “And David prepared iron in abundance for the nails for the doors of the gates, and for the joinings; and brass in abundance without weight” (1 Chronicles 22:3). Nails and joinings — the iron clamps and couplings that hold stone to stone and timber to timber. The Authorized Version uses joinings once, and it is a measure of how far down into the detail the preparation went. David's reason is given two verses later: “Solomon my son is young and tender, and the house that is to be builded for the LORD must be exceeding magnifical, of fame and of glory throughout all countries: I will therefore now make preparation for it. So David prepared abundantly before his death” (1 Chronicles 22:5). He laid up iron for joints he would never see fastened. The dictionary draws out what Scripture itself draws out of it: a man may be denied the work and still be given the preparation. David was told he would not build because he had shed blood, and he spent his last years buying brass without weight for his son's masons. Faithfulness often looks like stockpiling fasteners for a building somebody else will raise.

pos: n. pl. (arrangements; the appointed order of service)
etymology: Latin ordo, order, rank, series, through French ordre. In 1 Chronicles 24:19 it renders a Hebrew word for appointed offices or charges.
biblical_def: David, with Zadok and Ahimelech, divides the priests into twenty-four courses and assigns them by lot, and the chapter closes with a summary: “These were the orderings of them in their service to come into the house of the LORD, according to their manner, under Aaron their father, as the LORD God of Israel had commanded him” (1 Chronicles 24:19). Four things are packed into that sentence. The courses were orderings — fixed, assigned, written down. They governed coming into the house of the LORD. They followed the manner established under Aaron. And they rested on divine command. The Authorized Version uses orderings once. These are the courses Luke still assumes centuries later when he introduces Zacharias of the course of Abia, burning incense at the hour of prayer, which is where the gospel narrative opens. The dictionary reads the chapter as warrant for the plainest of worship principles: God appoints how He is approached. He did it by name and by lot in 1 Chronicles 24, and the regulative principle is simply that same conviction applied under the new covenant — what He commands in worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted there.

corruption_paragraphs: The modern settlement makes the shape of corporate worship a question of culture, preference, and effectiveness. 1 Chronicles 24 shows God appointing the courses, the manner, and the men. The principle to recover is that the orderings were not Aaron's invention or David's innovation — they were as the LORD God of Israel had commanded him. Luke 1:8 shows the arrangement still standing when the gospel opens, which is the strongest possible testimony to how durable divinely appointed order is.

pos: n. (the act of establishing; a settled or confirmed state)
etymology: Latin stabilire, to make firm, from stabilis, stable, through French establir. In 2 Chronicles 32:1 it denotes the settled state of Hezekiah's reformation.
biblical_def: The Chronicler sets Sennacherib's invasion immediately after Hezekiah's reforms, and the joint is one word: “After these things, and the establishment thereof, Sennacherib king of Assyria came, and entered into Judah, and encamped against the fenced cities, and thought to win them for himself” (2 Chronicles 32:1). These things are the cleansing of the temple, the restored passover, the smashed images, the reorganised priesthood. The establishment thereof means that the reformation held; it was not a gesture but a settled state. And then the Assyrian came. The Authorized Version uses establishment once. The dictionary notes carefully what the verse does not teach: that reformation purchases peace. Hezekiah did right and was invaded. What the reformation purchased was a king who could say the right thing when the invasion came: “With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us, and to fight our battles” (2 Chronicles 32:8). A church that has settled its doctrine before the trial arrives has not bought immunity; it has bought the ability to stand. The establishment of the reformation and the coming of Sennacherib belong in the same verse on purpose.

corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity reading cannot handle this verse. Hezekiah had done every work in the service of the house of God with all his heart, and the next sentence is Sennacherib encamping against the fenced cities. Scripture joins the two deliberately. Obedience is not a transaction, and the Chronicler's commendation of Hezekiah is not undone by the siege.

The principle to recover is what establishment is actually for. Because the reformation had settled, Hezekiah knew what to say when the Assyrian came, and the people rested themselves upon his words. Doctrine settled in peacetime is what a people stand on in war.

pos: n. (a judicial inquiry; careful inspection or questioning)
etymology: Latin examinare, to weigh or test, from examen, the tongue of a balance. In Acts 25:26 it renders the Greek anakrisis, a judicial investigation.
biblical_def: Festus has a prisoner he cannot classify and a report he cannot write: “Of whom I have no certain thing to write unto my lord. Wherefore I have brought him forth before you, and specially before thee, O king Agrippa, that, after examination had, I might have somewhat to write” (Acts 25:26). The Authorized Version uses examination once, and the Latin behind it is the tongue of a balance — to examine is to weigh. Festus wants Agrippa to weigh Paul so that Rome can be told something. What follows in Acts 26 is not an examination of Paul at all; it is the most complete statement of Paul's conversion and commission in Scripture, delivered to a king, with a Roman governor listening. Paul had already appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11), and the appeal that looked like a legal manoeuvre was the means by which the gospel went to Rome in chains and at imperial expense. The dictionary notes the pattern Scripture keeps showing: a hearing arranged to assess a Christian becomes a hearing at which Christ is preached. The believer under examination is not on trial alone; his examiners are.

corruption_paragraphs: The one error to name is quietist: the assumption that a Christian hauled before a magistrate should say as little as possible. Paul used every hearing to preach, and he used Roman law without apology — he appealed unto Caesar, he claimed his citizenship, and he turned an examination into an exposition of the resurrection.

Acts 25:26 is the only place the Authorized Version uses examination.
Festus needed something certain to write to his lord in Rome.
The examination became Paul's fullest account of his conversion and commission.

pos: adv. (in a pure manner; completely, thoroughly)
etymology: Latin purus, clean, unmixed, through French pur, with the ending -ly. In Isaiah 1:25 it carries the sense of thoroughly, to purity.
biblical_def: Isaiah has told Jerusalem what she has become — “Thy silver is become dross, thy wine mixed with water” (Isaiah 1:22) — and then declares what the LORD will do about it: “And I will turn my hand upon thee, and purely purge away thy dross, and take away all thy tin” (Isaiah 1:25). The metaphor is the refiner's furnace, and the adverb is the whole promise. Not partly purge; purely purge — thoroughly, to the point of purity, with the tin as well as the dross taken out. The Authorized Version uses purely once. The dictionary notes that the hand turned upon Jerusalem is a chastening hand, not a destroying one; the furnace is for silver and the silver is kept. This is the doctrine of sanctification stated in metal. God does not improve His people's alloy; He melts them and removes what is not silver, and the process is painful by design and complete by promise. The chapter's famous invitation stands a few verses earlier and belongs with it: “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18). Justification promises the white; sanctification promises the purging; and both are the LORD's own work, not the city's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PURELY, adverb In a pure manner; without mixture; innocently; merely; completely.
webster_full: PURELY, adverb In a pure manner; with an entire separation of heterogeneous matter.
2. Innocently; without guilt.
3. Merely; barely; completely.
PURE, adjective Separate from all heterogeneous or extraneous matter; clear; free from mixture.
2. Free from moral defilement; without spot; not sullied or tarnished; incorrupt; undebased by moral impurity; holy.

corruption_summary: Sanctification is widely reduced to gradual self-improvement; Isaiah 1:25 is a furnace, and the hand that turns upon the city is God's.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern account of growth in holiness is largely managerial: habits, disciplines, incremental progress, the believer as his own project. Isaiah 1:25 is a refiner's fire, and the subject of every verb is the LORD — I will turn my hand, I will purely purge, I will take away. Disciplines have their place as means, but the purging is His and it is thorough.

The principle to recover is that chastening is mercy. The hand turned upon Jerusalem was the hand of her God, the furnace was for silver, and the promise is purely — not a partial improvement but the removal of all the tin. Isaiah 1:18 holds the other half: sins as scarlet made white as snow.
roots_summary: From Latin purus, unmixed; in Isaiah 1:25 it means thoroughly, to purity — the refiner taking out dross and tin together.
roots_lines: Latin purus, clean, unmixed; French pur.
Isaiah 1:25 is the only place the Authorized Version uses purely.
The figure is the refiner's furnace: dross and tin removed from silver.
Isaiah 1:22 had named the corruption — silver become dross, wine mixed with water.
Every verb in the promise has the LORD as its subject.

I will turn my hand upon thee
